findings.title: Self-imposed prohibition as boundary crossing
findings.claim: When the focus form forbids the good that God has made lawful, the act of self-barring can itself become the transgression named at the end of the ayah.
findings.mechanism: The focus prohibition carrier meets exact wider connection rows at 66:1, 16:116, and 10:59 that return the same lawful-forbidden classification question to the human actor; this makes the two prohibitions read as a calibrated boundary rather than a command to maximize austerity.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees why the warning against transgression qualifies the ban on self-denial: stricter practice can cross the assigned limit when it redraws lawful status.
findings.containment: The finding preserves the ordinary prohibition on excess and the reality of declared restrictions; it concerns unauthorized reclassification of what is made lawful, not permission for every appetite.

epistemic.reason: The focus branch and exact connection rows are supplied, while the reader-walk source is legacy_unbound and the boundary-crossing conclusion remains an interpretive inference.

findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the prohibition as guarding who may classify a thing as sacredly permitted or forbidden, while the ordinary ethical limit remains visible.
findings.containment: This is an attributed contextual inference. The closing may also function as doxology, and no independent lexicon gloss or facet is asserted for the unresolved context branches.
